lesson: Cortisol and the adrenal gland — understand the normal

stages.title: Why does the body need cortisol?
stages.script:
Why does the body need cortisol?

You may have heard cortisol described as the stress hormone. But what does that actually mean? Why does the body need a stress hormone in the first place?

Cortisol helps the body to change priorities during physiological stress.

And when I say physiological stress, I mean the kinds of challenges humans have had to survive throughout evolution: periods without food, injury and infection.

lack of food first.

Even when there is no food coming in, the body still needs energy. The brain still needs glucose, muscles need fuel, and vital organs have to keep functioning. So this is not the time to store energy for later. Cortisol helps shift the body towards making its existing energy stores available.

In adipose tissue, cortisol promotes lipolysis. Stored triglycerides are broken down into free fatty acids and glycerol. The fatty acids can be used by many tissues as an alternative fuel. This helps spare glucose for tissues that depend on it more heavily, particularly the brain. The glycerol travels to the liver where it can be used to make new glucose.

In skeletal muscle, cortisol increases the breakdown of muscle protein, releasing amino acids, particularly alanine and glutamine, into the circulation. These amino acids also travel to the liver and provide more of the raw material needed for glucose production.

In the liver cortisol increases the production of key gluconeogenic enzymes. One of these is PEPCK, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, channels carbon from non-carbohydrate sources, such as amino acids, into the pathway that produces new glucose. Another one is glucose-6-phosphatase. This enzyme performs the final release step. It removes the phosphate from glucose-6-phosphate, producing free glucose that can leave the liver and enter the bloodstream.

Cortisol also opposes some of insulin's effects in muscle and adipose tissue: less glucose is taken up and stored by these tissues, leaving more glucose available in the circulation.

The overall effect is coordinated: adipose tissue releases fatty acids and glycerol, muscle supplies amino acids, and the liver turns these substrates into glucose and releases it into the blood.

Now think about injury or serious illness.

Whatever else is happening, blood still has to reach the brain, heart and other vital organs. Cortisol helps maintain vascular tone and helps blood vessels respond appropriately to catecholamines such as adrenaline and noradrenaline. In other words, it helps support the circulation when the body is under stress.

And infection presents another challenge.

We need inflammation to fight infection. But inflammation is powerful, and if that response becomes excessive, it can begin to damage our own tissues.

So the body needs to achieve a balance: fight the infection strongly enough, but don't allow the inflammatory response itself to become uncontrolled.

And there is an interesting feedback system that helps achieve this.

During infection, inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha signal to the brain that there is significant inflammation in the body. The brain responds by activating the hormonal pathway that increases cortisol production.

As cortisol rises, it acts back on the immune system through glucocorticoid receptors, reducing the production of further pro-inflammatory signals.

So the inflammatory response actually helps trigger one of its own brakes.

We'll come back later to exactly how the brain controls cortisol production. For now, the important thing is to understand why this response is useful.

When you look at cortisol's different actions, they can initially seem unrelated.

It makes energy available.

It supports the circulation.

And it helps prevent inflammation from becoming excessive.

But these aren't simply three random effects of the same hormone. They are all part of the same overall strategy.

Cortisol helps the body change its priorities so that it can adapt to physiological stress.

That's the idea I want you to keep in mind when thinking about cortisol throughout this lesson.

stages.title: Adrenal anatomy
stages.script: First give cortisol a physical home. The adrenal glands are small endocrine organs that sit on the upper poles of the kidneys. Each adrenal gland has two major regions: an outer cortex and an inner medulla. These are not simply different layers of the same tissue. They are functionally distinct endocrine systems. The adrenal cortex makes steroid hormones. Moving from outside inward, the zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone, the zona fasciculata makes cortisol, and the zona reticularis contributes adrenal androgens. The central medulla is different again. Its chromaffin cells are closely related to the sympathetic nervous system and release catecholamines, mainly adrenaline and noradrenaline. For this lesson, the important location is the broad middle cortical layer: the zona fasciculata. That is where cortisol is made. So already we have a useful mental map. Adrenal gland above the kidney. Cortex on the outside. Medulla in the middle. And within the cortex, the zona fasciculata is the main home of cortisol. Whenever we later talk about ACTH stimulating cortisol production, picture ACTH arriving at this middle cortical layer rather than thinking of the adrenal as one undifferentiated organ.

stages.title: A steroid hormone
stages.script: Now move from anatomy to chemistry, but only as far as the chemistry helps us understand the physiology. Cortisol is a steroid hormone, and every adrenal steroid starts from cholesterol. The adrenal cortex takes cholesterol and, through a series of enzymatic steps, converts it into different steroid hormones. We could spend a long time memorising that synthesis pathway, but for a Fundamentals lesson the more important idea is this: cortisol is derived from cholesterol and is therefore lipid soluble. That changes how it behaves. Unlike many peptide hormones, cortisol can cross the cell membrane. It does not need a surface receptor to pass a message inward. It can enter the cell and bind an intracellular glucocorticoid receptor. Steroid hormones are also not stored in large secretory vesicles in the same way as insulin, for example. The adrenal largely makes cortisol when it is needed. So the control system regulates synthesis itself. Keep that distinction in mind. Cortisol is not merely a molecule floating in the blood. Its chemical nature explains how it crosses membranes, how it reaches receptors inside cells and why changes in production can influence many tissues throughout the body.

stages.title: How cortisol acts
stages.script: So what happens when cortisol reaches a target cell? Because it is lipid soluble, cortisol can cross the plasma membrane. Inside the cell it binds the glucocorticoid receptor. The hormone-receptor complex then moves into the nucleus, where it interacts with DNA and with other transcription factors. The result is a change in gene transcription. Some genes are switched up, others are suppressed, and the pattern depends on the tissue and the physiological context. This is one reason cortisol has such wide-ranging effects. It can influence enzymes involved in glucose production in the liver, proteins that determine vascular responsiveness, inflammatory signalling pathways, bone turnover, muscle metabolism and growth. It also explains why many cortisol effects are not instantaneous in the way an ion channel opening is instantaneous. The hormone changes the cell's programme of protein expression. There are also faster non-genomic effects, but for understanding most everyday physiology the intracellular receptor and gene-transcription model is the key one. So when we say cortisol has effects throughout the body, there is a common mechanism underneath: a cholesterol-derived steroid crosses the membrane, binds its receptor and changes how the cell expresses genes.

stages.title: HPA axis
stages.script: Now we need the control system. Cortisol production is governed mainly by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, usually shortened to the HPA axis. Start in the hypothalamus. It releases corticotropin-releasing hormone, CRH. CRH travels through the pituitary portal circulation to the anterior pituitary, where it stimulates corticotroph cells to release ACTH, adrenocorticotropic hormone. ACTH then travels in the systemic circulation to the adrenal cortex, particularly the zona fasciculata, and stimulates cortisol synthesis. But the system is not simply a three-step chain. Cortisol feeds back negatively on both the pituitary and the hypothalamus. If cortisol is plentiful, CRH and ACTH drive are reduced. If cortisol falls, that negative feedback is removed, so the brain and pituitary try to stimulate the adrenal more strongly. This feedback loop is extremely useful clinically because it lets us reason about where a defect sits. If the adrenal itself fails and cortisol falls, ACTH should rise. If the problem is upstream in the pituitary or hypothalamus, ACTH may be low or inappropriately normal. Before going further, use the feedback loop. If the adrenal gland fails and cortisol becomes low, what should happen to ACTH?

feedback.correct: Correct. Low cortisol removes negative feedback from the pituitary and hypothalamus, so ACTH rises when the adrenal itself is the failing organ.
feedback.wrong: Think about negative feedback. If cortisol falls, its inhibitory signal to the pituitary is removed. In primary adrenal failure, ACTH therefore rises rather than falls.

stages.title: Rhythm and stress
stages.script: Cortisol is not secreted at one fixed level throughout the day. It follows a strong circadian rhythm. In a person with a normal sleep-wake cycle, cortisol begins to rise in the hours before waking, reaches its highest levels around the early morning, and then gradually declines through the day. Levels are usually lowest around midnight. Superimposed on this daily rhythm are pulses of secretion and, importantly, responses to physiological stress. Infection, trauma, surgery, fasting, hypoglycaemia and severe illness all increase HPA-axis activity. In those situations the body raises cortisol output because the demands on metabolism and circulation have changed. This is why calling cortisol simply a stress hormone is not quite enough. Cortisol has important everyday functions even when nothing dramatic is happening. But during physiological stress, the body increases that normal system to preserve function when the environment becomes more difficult. This also matters when interpreting cortisol measurements. A level that might be appropriate late at night could be inadequate during major illness. The key idea is therefore time and context: cortisol output is dynamic, it follows a daily rhythm, and it increases when the body needs extra physiological support.

stages.title: Fuel availability
stages.script: The first major job to understand is fuel availability. Imagine a child who has been vomiting, has not eaten, and then develops a serious infection. The brain and other essential tissues still require usable energy even though no meal is arriving. Cortisol helps solve that problem. In the liver it supports gluconeogenesis: the production of glucose from non-carbohydrate substrates. It also helps mobilise amino acids from protein and fatty acids from adipose tissue, making metabolic fuel and gluconeogenic substrate available. The purpose is not simply to make the blood glucose high. The purpose is to prevent circulating fuel from falling dangerously when intake is poor or demand rises. That is why cortisol becomes particularly important during fasting, infection and illness. It also explains two apparently opposite clinical findings. Severe cortisol deficiency can cause hypoglycaemia, especially in children, because the normal fasting and stress response is lost. Chronic cortisol excess can push glucose in the opposite direction and contribute to hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance. So from one physiological role, maintaining fuel availability, we can derive two different pathological directions. Now make the prediction from the normal physiology. During illness, what becomes more likely if cortisol is severely deficient?

feedback.correct: Exactly. Without adequate cortisol, hepatic glucose support during fasting and illness is reduced, so hypoglycaemia becomes more likely, particularly in children.
feedback.wrong: That pattern fits cortisol excess better. Severe cortisol deficiency removes part of the normal fasting and stress response, so hypoglycaemia is the direction to expect.

stages.title: Protein and fat
stages.script: Where does the body get the material it needs to maintain fuel supply during stress? Part of the answer is from stored tissue. Cortisol promotes protein catabolism in peripheral tissues, especially muscle, releasing amino acids that can be used by the liver for gluconeogenesis and by the body for higher-priority processes. It also promotes mobilisation of fatty acids from adipose tissue. In an acute stress situation, this redistribution of resources is adaptive. The body is effectively saying: immediate survival takes priority over building muscle or storing energy. But the same physiology becomes harmful if cortisol exposure stays high for weeks or months. Persistent protein catabolism contributes to proximal muscle weakness and loss of lean tissue. Connective tissue becomes fragile, contributing to thin skin and easy bruising. In children, chronic cortisol excess interferes with normal growth. Fat metabolism also changes, and prolonged excess produces the characteristic redistribution of adipose tissue seen in Cushing syndrome. The useful principle is that the body is temporarily reallocating resources during stress. Short term, that helps. Long term, the cost of continually breaking down and redistributing tissue becomes clinically visible.

stages.title: Blood pressure
stages.script: The next job is easy to underestimate but crucial in adrenal insufficiency: cortisol helps the cardiovascular system respond appropriately to catecholamines. Adrenaline and noradrenaline can constrict blood vessels and support blood pressure, but normal cortisol has a permissive effect on that response. It helps maintain the expression and function of adrenergic receptors and supports vascular responsiveness. So imagine severe cortisol deficiency. The sympathetic nervous system may still release catecholamines, and we may even give exogenous catecholamines in an intensive care setting, but the vessels do not respond normally. Vascular tone falls and hypotension becomes harder to correct. That is one reason adrenal crisis can produce profound circulatory collapse. In primary adrenal failure, the situation may be made worse by simultaneous aldosterone deficiency, causing sodium loss and volume depletion. But cortisol itself contributes independently through this permissive effect on the circulation. Again the physiology predicts the pathology. Normal cortisol helps blood vessels respond to the signals that maintain vascular tone. Too little cortisol therefore predisposes to hypotension. Chronic cortisol excess can push the system in the opposite direction and contribute to hypertension. The important phrase to remember is not simply blood pressure. It is vascular responsiveness to catecholamines.

stages.title: Inflammation
stages.script: Another major role of cortisol is to restrain inflammation. Inflammation is not bad. It is essential for fighting infection, clearing damaged tissue and coordinating repair. But an inflammatory response that is too strong or continues unchecked can itself damage the body. Cortisol acts as one of the physiological brakes. Through the glucocorticoid receptor it suppresses transcription of many inflammatory mediators, interferes with signalling pathways such as NF-kappa-B and AP-one, and reduces production of multiple cytokines. It also changes leukocyte trafficking and function. The broad principle is more important than every molecular detail: cortisol prevents the inflammatory system from overshooting. During stress, that helps keep the response proportionate. But again there is a cost if exposure is excessive for too long. Chronic glucocorticoid excess suppresses immune function, increases susceptibility to infection and impairs wound healing. This is also why pharmacological glucocorticoids are so useful in inflammatory and autoimmune disease: we exploit a normal physiological action of cortisol and amplify it. So the anti-inflammatory effects of steroids are not an artificial drug effect. They are an extension of what endogenous cortisol normally does.

stages.title: Bone, growth and brain
stages.script: Cortisol also influences tissues that matter over longer time scales: bone, connective tissue, growth and the brain. At physiological levels, cortisol participates in normal regulation. The problems become obvious when exposure is chronically excessive. In bone, glucocorticoid excess reduces bone formation and alters calcium handling, so bone strength falls. In muscle and connective tissue, sustained catabolism produces weakness, skin thinning and easy bruising. In children, chronic cortisol excess suppresses linear growth. That paediatric point is particularly useful because a child gaining weight while linear growth slows should immediately make us think beyond simple obesity. Cortisol excess can also influence sleep, mood, attention and cognition because glucocorticoid receptors are widely expressed in the brain. None of these effects needs to be memorised as an isolated list. They all follow from the same broader idea: cortisol changes how tissues allocate energy and how strongly they pursue growth, repair and inflammatory activity. That is useful during acute stress, when survival takes priority. It is damaging when the body is exposed to the same signal continuously. Acute adaptation becomes chronic cost.

stages.title: Too little vs too much
stages.script: Now we can do something more useful than memorising Addison disease on one page and Cushing syndrome on another. Take the normal physiological roles and run them in opposite directions. Normal cortisol supports glucose availability. Therefore too little predisposes to hypoglycaemia, while too much promotes hyperglycaemia. Normal cortisol supports vascular responsiveness to catecholamines. Therefore too little contributes to hypotension and shock, while chronic excess can contribute to hypertension. Normal cortisol mobilises protein and fat during stress. Therefore chronic excess causes muscle wasting, tissue fragility and altered fat distribution. Normal cortisol restrains inflammation. Therefore too much suppresses immune responses and impairs healing. Normal cortisol influences bone and growth. Therefore chronic excess reduces bone formation and suppresses growth. This is the central teaching point of the whole lesson. Once you understand what cortisol normally does, most of the manifestations of deficiency and excess are simply the normal physiology pushed too far in one direction or removed in the other. Before the final reconstruction, choose the pattern that follows most directly from cortisol deficiency: hypoglycaemia with hypotension, or hyperglycaemia with hypertension?

feedback.correct: Correct. Deficiency removes glucose support and reduces vascular responsiveness, so hypoglycaemia and hypotension are the directions predicted by the physiology.
feedback.wrong: That pattern fits cortisol excess. With deficiency, glucose support and vascular responsiveness fall, so think hypoglycaemia and hypotension.

stages.title: Reconstruct the system
stages.script: Now rebuild the whole system once, from first principles. The adrenal glands sit above the kidneys. The adrenal cortex makes steroid hormones, and cortisol is produced mainly in the zona fasciculata. Cortisol is made from cholesterol. Because it is lipid soluble, it crosses cell membranes, binds the intracellular glucocorticoid receptor and changes gene transcription. The hypothalamus releases CRH, the pituitary releases ACTH, and ACTH stimulates the adrenal to make cortisol. Cortisol then feeds back negatively on both hypothalamus and pituitary. Production follows a circadian rhythm and increases during physiological stress. What is the body trying to achieve? Preserve fuel availability. Mobilise metabolic substrate when necessary. Maintain vascular responsiveness to catecholamines. Restrain excessive inflammation. Coordinate longer-term effects on tissue maintenance, bone and growth. Then run the model in either direction. Remove cortisol and you predict failure of fasting and stress adaptation, hypoglycaemia and hypotension. Expose the body to too much cortisol for too long and the same normal actions become hyperglycaemia, muscle wasting, growth suppression, reduced bone formation and immune suppression. That is the point of the Fundamentals lesson: not to remember a longer list, but to understand the normal system well enough that the pathology can be derived from it.
